analysis.one_liner: Writes net neutrality into law: broadband providers could not block or discriminate against lawful internet traffic.
analysis.headline: The bill to write net neutrality into law was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write 'net neutrality' rules into statute. Internet providers like cable and wireless companies could not block lawful websites or apps, could not unjustly or unreasonably slow or discriminate in how they deliver lawful traffic, and would have to plainly disclose their prices, speeds, and network management practices. The Federal Communications Commission would enforce these rules by hearing complaints and could fine willful violators up to $2 million per practice. The bill also bars the FCC from reclassifying broadband under Title II of the Communications Act, the stricter legal framework used in earlier FCC net neutrality rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers benefit: they would gain a legal guarantee that their internet provider cannot block lawful content or discriminate against lawful traffic, and must disclose real prices and performance. Websites, streaming services, small online businesses, and app developers also benefit, since their traffic could not be slowed or blocked by the cable and wireless companies that control the pipes.

how_it_helps.text: It bans broadband providers from blocking lawful content, applications, services, or non-harmful devices, subject to reasonable network management.
It bars providers from unjustly or unreasonably discriminating in how they transmit lawful internet traffic, which targets throttling of particular sites or services.
It requires providers to disclose clear, accurate information about price, performance, and network management so consumers can compare services and internet companies can build new offerings.
It lets the FCC fine a willful violator up to $2 million per practice and issue injunctions against blocking or discrimination.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband internet providers — cable, telephone, and wireless companies — would bear the cost: they could no longer block, throttle, or discriminate among lawful traffic, could not charge content companies for preferential treatment, and would face compliance, disclosure, and potential fine exposure up to $2 million per violating practice.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable, phone, and wireless broadband companies

drawbacks.text: Enforcement depends entirely on FCC complaint adjudication — consumers get no private right of action in court, so each case would be a slow regulatory proceeding rather than a lawsuit.
Fines are capped at $2 million per violating practice, which is small relative to the revenues of the largest broadband companies and may not deter violations.

The bill blocks the FCC from imposing Title II (common-carrier) regulations on broadband, locking in a lighter-touch regime and preventing stronger rules that other net neutrality proposals would allow.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give consumers legal protection against ISPs blocking or throttling lawful content at essentially no cost to the public, though its complaint-based enforcement, low fine cap, and lack of a private right of action make it weaker than fuller net neutrality proposals; critics would also note it shields ISPs from broader FCC regulation. Its practical significance ended when it died in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never moved, never got a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Latta introduced the bill on February 6, 2019, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote in either chamber.
The bill died in committee at the end of the 116th Congress without becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers are better off because the bill died: no statutory net neutrality obligations were created, so the companies kept the legal freedom to manage, prioritize, or slow lawful traffic as they choose.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadband providers, freed of net neutrality obligations

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no markup, no vote, and no report to the House.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with 18 Republican cosponsors, but because it never reached a vote, the record shows no floor opposition or roll-call split.

industries.industry: Broadband internet providers (cable, telephone, and wireless carriers)
industries.note: The bill would bar them from blocking, throttling, or discriminating among lawful traffic and require public disclosure of pricing and network practices, forfeiting the option to charge content companies for prioritized delivery. In exchange, they gain statutory limits on FCC authority, since the bill bars Title II common-carrier regulation.

industries.industry: Internet content, application, and device companies
industries.note: Websites, streaming services, and app makers rely on equal access to consumers and would benefit from rules preventing ISPs from degrading or blocking their traffic. The bill requires disclosure of network practices so these companies can market new offerings.
